# PART 1 – Credibility and open research {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1 – 90 minutes
:::

::: notes
Part one, then. We start further back than you might expect, with what science is for, why anyone thinks it is in trouble, and the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset and disagreed. Then the vocabulary that separates three kinds of repetition, the practices that open research proposes as a remedy, and the evidence: three very large studies, published together, that measured how often social-science findings survive being repeated, one of which supplies the case of today. We finish on the infrastructure, the software, archives and registries without which open research would be a slogan, and on opening the browser lab, where all of today's work happens.
:::

## What social science is for {#what-are-we-doing-when-we-do-social-science}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is offered to others so that they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science depends on that handover, and everything that follows is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
Start with the obvious question that nobody asks out loud: what are we actually doing when we do social science? We are making claims about the world – claims that could turn out to be wrong, and that come with some statement of how we would find out. And you publish a claim so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it, and build on top of it. The whole enterprise depends on that handover, and a finding that nobody else can examine remains an assertion. So when we ask whether social science is in trouble, the question is quite specific. Does the handover work, and can someone else pick your finding up and do anything with it?
:::

## False positives and forking paths {#three-arguments-that-made-people-nervous .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments made people nervous, and I take them in order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis in 2005 made the theoretical case: put together small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and lots of teams chasing the same question, and you can show that most published findings in a field will be false without anybody breaking a single rule. Then Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn demonstrated it in practice – give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have, and you can push a five per cent false-positive rate above sixty. They proved it by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes you younger. And Gelman and Loken added the subtlety that I find hardest to shake: you do not have to run many tests for this to bite. If the one test you ran was chosen after you looked at the data, its p-value is already wrong.
:::

## Evidence from replications and many-analysts studies {#and-then-people-counted .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology studies**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields and different designs. In the first, **most findings were not significant again in new samples**; in the second, **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
And then people stopped arguing and counted. The Open Science Collaboration took a hundred psychology studies and replicated them properly – high power, original materials, the original authors consulted where possible. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result. Thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half the original size. That is the study that made 'replication crisis' a phrase outside methodology seminars. The second one is closest to home, because it is ours: seventy-three teams, their members mostly sociologists and political scientists, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. Different fields and different designs. In the first, most findings were not significant again when the studies were rerun on new samples; in the second, the finding depended on who did the analysis.
:::

## Incentives and questionable research practices {#it-is-not-mostly-fraud .smaller}

::: {.small}
Fraud exists, but it is rare. The mechanism behind these results is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these ordinary practices [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person, so the problem cannot be fixed by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
This is not mostly a story about fraud, and I want to be emphatic about that. Fraud exists and it is spectacular when it surfaces, but it is rare and it is not what these numbers are measuring. The mechanism is ordinary and it is structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small, individually defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data, because how else would you make them. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader sees one path through a garden with hundreds. And in most cases neither the data nor the code are available, so nobody can check any of it. John, Loewenstein and Prelec went and asked researchers directly, anonymously, with a mechanism designed to make truthful answers worth giving – and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. Not one of those steps requires a bad actor, and that is why the problem is hard: you cannot solve it by hiring better people. [pause] So suppose you did hire the best people you could find, gave them all the same data and the same question, and watched what they did.
:::

## The red-card study {#twenty-nine-teams-one-question .smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the first many-analysts study. Every one since is a variation on it, including Multi100, from which this course takes its case.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
Silberzahn and colleagues ran something very close to that experiment, in a study published in twenty eighteen, and every many-analysts study since, including the one I took part in, is a variation on its design. The question is concrete: are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones? The data went to everyone identically – two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the three thousand referees they had played under, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player-referee pairs, with skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who were not told the research question. And then the design: twenty-nine teams analysed it independently, reviewed each other's approaches before anybody had seen a single result, revised, and only then compared answers. Nobody could tune their method to get a number they liked, because nobody knew what number anyone was getting.
:::

## 'Replication' crises

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Another 'replication' crisis – terminological confusion?
:::
::: {.fragment}
The term 'reproducibility' has been used as a synonym for a number of different characteristics – reproducibility, robustness, replicability, repeatability, credibility, and trustworthiness [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms, p. 2].
:::
[[Successfully rerun the same code on the same data?]{colour="#b22222"}]{.fragment}
[[Re-analyse the same data a different way?]{colour="#1C69A8"}]{.fragment}
[[Collect fresh data and analyse it in the same way?]{colour="#4D179A"}]{.fragment}
[[Using the same data and same analysis but asking a different question?]{colour="#3C6301"}]{.fragment}
[[Asking the same question but answering it with fresh data and a different analysis?]{colour="#3BB8DB"}]{.fragment}
::::

::: notes
So twenty-nine competent teams worked on one dataset and did not agree. What I have not said yet is what *kind* of failure that is, and part of the difficulty is the word itself. For years 'replication' covered everything: rerunning someone's code, re-analysing their data a different way, collecting new data altogether. Those are three different operations, answering three different questions, but because we called them all 'replication', the crisis debates had people talking past each other for a decade. So before any more numbers, we need the vocabulary.
:::

## Repeatability and credibility {#credibility-is-not-truth}

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.9; --lh: 1.15"}
"**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated."

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

"For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence."
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms [p. 2]
:::

::: notes
The glossary on this slide is worth reading slowly, because it separates two things we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella: reproducibility, robustness and replicability as a family, all asking whether the answer survives repeating some step of the process. Credibility and trustworthiness are about how much confidence a finding deserves – and note the sentence in the middle. Because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth. A credible finding can be wrong. What credibility is built from is the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them. That last one is the one we will keep coming back to.
:::

## Quick check – the matrix in peer review {#quick-check-credibility-in-the-wild .questionslide transition="fade-in none-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

- 'Reviewer 1' wants to ensure that your results are [reproducible]{.fragment .bounceIn}, so she sources your R script to run the entire analysis. You're in luck – she hasn't yet updated her `dplyr`, so the code runs.
- 'Reviewer 2' is very eager. He's unconvinced by your modelling choices, so he fits your data to another function to check if your findings are truly [robust]{.fragment .bounceIn}. You're in luck again – he recovers your point estimate to a reasonable precision, although the confidence intervals have widened.
- 'Reviewer 3' takes a special interest because he's just working on a similar paper on data they published recently. Do your results [replicate]{.fragment .bounceIn} when your methods are applied to that state-of-the-art dataset?
:::

::: notes
Here is the matrix at work on one paper. You submit a paper with its replication package, and three reviewers each check something different. For each one, call out or type in the chat which cell of the matrix that reviewer is in, before the answer appears. Reviewer 1 reruns your own script on your own data. [pause] [advance] Reproduction. Reviewer 2 fits your data with a different function. [pause] [advance] Robustness. Reviewer 3 applies your methods to a dataset that somebody else published. [pause] [advance] Replication.
:::

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start – your code, your data, your materials. Open research is a list of practices that supply those things and more, each of which removes a specific, identifiable obstacle. Open data means someone else can re-analyse your evidence rather than taking your word for it. Open code means they can rerun your exact analysis. Open materials means they can run the study again in a new sample. Open access means they can read the thing at all, which sounds trivial until you try to get a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist. And registered reports go further: the plan is peer-reviewed and the publication decision is made before anyone sees a result, which removes the incentive to find something. Each removes one obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. Whether published findings hold up when somebody does check them has now been measured on a large scale.
:::

## The SCORE programme {#what-is-score}

::: {.small}
- DARPA-funded programme to gauge the credibility of social-science claims
- A stratified sample of papers from **62 journals**, published **2009–2018**
- The central claim of each paper traced from the abstract to the statistic that supports it
- Thousands of researchers, and three repetition studies built on the same sampling frame
:::

::: notes
The three papers we look at next all come from one programme, SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence. It was funded, oddly enough, by DARPA, the research agency of the US Department of Defense, which wanted to know whether you could predict which findings hold up. It starts from a stratified sample of papers from sixty-two journals, published between 2009 and 2018, and traces the central claim of each paper from the abstract down to the statistic that supports it. The three studies then took that same sampling frame and each asked one of our three questions. So the numbers you are about to hear all describe the same body of literature, asked three different things.
:::

## Reproducibility – Miske et al.

::: {.small}
- **600 papers** sampled (62 journals, 2009–2018)
- Ask the authors for data and code, then try to rerun the reported result
- How often is that even possible?
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
Reproducibility is the gentlest test of the three. The design in one breath: take six hundred papers, ask the authors for their data and code, and try to recompute the central reported result from the same data with the same analysis. Before we ask how often that works, the first finding is about how rarely you can even start.
:::

## Data availability – Miske et al. {#why-some-fields-do-better}

::: {.small}
- Journals with a sharing policy: **66.2–100%** data availability vs **16.0%** without
- By discipline: **54.1%** data availability in political science vs **2.9%** in education
- With data *and* code: **90.9%** approximately reproducible vs **38.1%** from rebuilt source data
:::

::: {.claimcard}
"The most substantial barrier … was the unavailability of author data."

"Reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct."
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
And access follows policy. Where journals have a data-sharing policy, availability runs from about two thirds to one hundred per cent, depending on the policy; without one, it is sixteen. Political science and economics built the habit early and are far ahead of the rest. The first quote is the conclusion of the paper itself – the biggest barrier was simply that the data were not there. The second quote is the one to remember: "reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct." Reproducing a number tells you that the computation was faithful, and nothing about whether the claim about the world is true.
:::

## Robustness – Aczel et al. (Multi100)

::: {.small}
- **100 studies**, each re-analysed by **≥5 independent analysts**
- The same data for every analyst, each free to choose any *justifiable* analysis
- A peer panel judges whether each pipeline is appropriate
- I was one of its analysts, on a different paper from the one we work on today
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness.
:::

::: notes
The middle paper is the one I was in, as an analyst of a different paper from the one we work on today. One hundred studies, and for each one at least five analysts working independently: no teams, original authors barred, everyone handed the same data and the same claim. You were free to analyse it any way you could justify, and a peer panel later judged whether your pipeline was appropriate. Most of the hundred studies had passed a reproducibility check first, and any that failed one was dropped, so robustness was measured mostly on reproducible material. For nine of them the reproduction was never attempted, and the paper that we work on today is one of the nine.
:::

## Robustness results – Aczel et al. {#same-data-five-analysts-different-answers}

::: {.small}
- **34%** of reanalysis effect sizes within ±0.05 *d* of the original (57% within ±0.20)
- **74%** reached the same conclusion, 24% a null or inconclusive one, **2%** the opposite
- Effect sizes shrank: original mean *d* **0.73** → reanalysis **0.49**
- Analyst-to-analyst variability typically **exceeds** sampling error
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness.
:::

::: notes
Free, justifiable choices on the same data move the answer a long way. Only about a third of the reanalyses fell within five hundredths of a Cohen's d of the original, and in just five studies out of ninety-five did all the analysts come that close. Conclusions held up better than magnitudes, with three quarters of reanalyses agreeing with the original conclusion. But the effect sizes shrank, from a mean d of point seven three down to point four nine. The finding I keep coming back to is that the spread across analysts is typically larger than the statistical uncertainty inside any single analysis. The analyst, in other words, is a bigger source of noise than the sample. One more detail: observational studies came out less robust than experiments, which is worth remembering when we reach the design of our own case.
:::

- The strictest test: does the effect reappear in data that the original study did not use?

## The three Rs across SCORE {#the-three-rs-do-not-travel-together}

:::: {.none}
Reproducible ≠ robust ≠ replicable.

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Across SCORE the three are [**essentially uncorrelated**]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – knowing one barely predicts the others.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
So there is no single number for 'trust'. You have to ask *which* repetition you mean.
:::
::::

::: notes
You would hope these three properties go together – that a reproducible finding is more likely to be robust, and a robust one more likely to replicate. Across SCORE, and to my surprise, they do not. Measured on the same body of papers, the three indicators are essentially uncorrelated – knowing one tells you almost nothing about the others. So there is no single trust score for a finding. "Is it reliable?" is an incomplete question until you say which kind of repetition you mean. So for any one paper the useful question is which of the three tests it has been put through and how it fared, and that is the question we will put to the paper of today.
:::

## The two Multi100 tasks {#two-tasks-months-apart .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 1 – free reanalysis.** Reanalyse the claim however you see fit, then record one conclusion: evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
**Task 2 – constrained reanalysis.** Once Task 1 was in, instructions arrived: report a single main result from the family of *z*, *t*, *F* or $\chi^2$ tests (or an alternative or non-parametric version), with an instruction for each claim that fixed one or two details of the analysis.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Task 1 measures whether analysts reach the same verdict. Task 2 makes their *numbers* comparable, since five answers to five different questions cannot be averaged.
:::

::: notes
The study ran in two stages, and the distinction matters for everything that follows. Task one was complete freedom: reanalyse the claim however you see fit, and record one categorical conclusion out of four, evidence for the claim, evidence for the opposite, no evidence either way, or evidence for the null hypothesis. [advance] Once that was submitted, task two arrived. It asked for a single main result in the form of a test statistic, and it came with a short instruction for each claim that pinned down one or two details of the analysis. [advance] The order matters because the two tasks measure different things. Task one asks whether independent analysts reach the same verdict. Task two asks whether they produce the same number, and that question can only be asked once everyone is answering roughly the same question, which is what the instructions were for. We will read the instruction for our own claim later.
:::

## Results on a common scale {#how-a-hundred-studies-become-one-number .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Every analyst reports a test statistic in whatever form the model produces – **t**, **z**, **F**, $\chi^2$ – with its degrees of freedom or its sample size
- Each is converted to a **partial correlation** *r* and a standardised **Cohen's *d***, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R can be read on one axis
- A **peer panel** judges whether each pipeline is an appropriate analysis of the claim
- Only then can you ask how far apart several defensible answers are
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Standardising makes the comparison possible, but it assumes that the analysts are estimating **the same quantity**, and that the numbers fed into each conversion count the units that carry the evidence. Hold both thoughts.
:::

::: notes
Even with the question pinned down, the answers arrive in different forms. Everyone reports the test statistic that their model happens to produce, a t, a z, an F or a chi-square, with its degrees of freedom or its sample size. Multi100 converted those onto a common scale, a partial correlation and a standardised difference, so that a regression fitted in Stata and a test computed in R could be placed on the same axis. Alongside that, a peer panel judged whether each pipeline was an appropriate analysis of the claim at all, so the spread that comes out of the study is a spread among analyses that passed review. [advance] Putting several numbers on one axis takes two things for granted. One is that they estimate the same quantity, and a good deal of what follows is about what happens when they do not. The other is that each conversion counts the units that actually carry the evidence.
:::

## Licences, briefly {.smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

::: {.small}
| What | Common choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | MIT or GPL | MIT: use it however you like. GPL: and share your changes back |
| **Data** | CC0 or CC BY | CC0 puts it in the public domain; CC BY asks for attribution |
| **Text, figures, slides** | CC BY or CC BY-NC | Attribution, optionally no commercial reuse |
| **Someone else's data** | *their* terms | Licensed survey microdata usually may not be passed on, by me or by you |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Publishing with no licence is not a neutral default. It means **all rights reserved** – legally, nobody may reuse the work at all.
:::

::: notes
Licensing gets skipped and then bites. Four rows. For code, MIT says use it however you like, GPL says use it and share your changes back. For data, CC-zero puts it in the public domain and CC-BY asks for attribution. For text and figures and slides, CC-BY or CC-BY with a non-commercial clause. And the fourth row is the one that most often constrains a reanalysis: when the data are not yours, their terms govern. Much survey microdata is held under a licence that lets you analyse it and forbids you to pass it on, so a replication package can carry the code and point to the archive, but not the file itself. A dataset released under CC-zero, by contrast, can travel with the code, and anyone can rerun the analysis without asking anyone. ## The question of the paper {#the-question-of-the-paper .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The question.** Do the officials who control access to a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Officials who deal with the public directly, and decide how much help to give, are **street-level bureaucrats** [@Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy]
- **The method.** An **audit study** sends matched requests, or matched applicants, that differ in one characteristic, and compares what comes back [@BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg; @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord]. Here the characteristic is a name
- **What it added.** Audits of politicians and local election officials had found discrimination [@ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate; @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote]. This one asks about a bureaucracy that hands out a valuable benefit and is less tied to politics
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The paper is an experiment published in 2017 [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. From here on I call its two authors **the original authors (OAs)**.
:::

::: notes
The case of the day is a paper in the American Journal of Political Science, and I will call its two authors the original authors, or OAs, from here on, because the course is about the claim and its analyses rather than about the people who made it. The question is old and important: do the officials who stand between citizens and a public programme answer people differently by race or ethnicity? Sociologists call those officials street-level bureaucrats, after Lipsky, because they deal with the public directly and have discretion over how much help to give. The method is the audit study, which sends matched requests that differ in one characteristic and compares the responses. Earlier audits had found discrimination by politicians and election officials. The OAs asked whether the same holds in a bureaucracy that hands out something valuable, access to public housing, and is further from politics.
:::

::: {.small}
- The name was assigned **at random**, so no arrow points into it
- Only a reply can greet the sender by name: **name → reply → greeting**
- The **official**, whom nobody observed, and the **community** both affect whether a reply comes and how it opens
- The dashed arc is the claim, the arrow that Task 2 leaves for you to switch on
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Here is the experiment as a causal graph, the same graph that you finish in Task 2. On the left, the name, which was assigned by a random number generator, so nothing points into it, and that is what makes this an experiment. The name can change whether the official replies at all, and only a reply can greet the sender by name, so there is a chain from the name through the reply to the greeting. Above, the official, drawn pale because nobody observed them: workload, habits of courtesy, attitudes, anything about the person who reads the email, which affects both whether they reply and how they open. ## Comparing among replies {#comparing-among-replies .smaller}

- The reply is a **consequence of the name**, and a common effect of the name and the official: a **collider**

::::

::: {.fragment .small}
Conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change is **post-treatment conditioning**: the gap among replies mixes an effect on **how** officials write with a difference in **which** officials wrote [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment; @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias].
:::

::: notes
Now draw a box around the reply, because that is what the paper does when it compares greetings among replies only. The reply is caused by the name, and also by the official, so it is a common effect of the two, a collider. Conditioning on a collider opens a path between its causes: among the replies, the name and the official are no longer independent. If a Hispanic name discourages some officials from replying, the officials who answered Santiago are a different mix from those who answered Brett, perhaps the more conscientious ones, perhaps the busier ones. Their habits of greeting then travel along the red path into the comparison. [advance] The general name for this is post-treatment conditioning, conditioning on something that the treatment can change, and it can produce a gap even where the name has no effect on tone at all. Coppock wrote about it for exactly this kind of audit experiment.
:::

## Counting every delivered email {#counting-every-delivered-email .smaller}

::: {.small}
- Count **every delivered email**, with no reply counted as no greeting: no box, nothing opened, and the groups stay as randomisation made them
- The outcome changes with it: a **reply that greets the sender by name**, which combines whether a reply came with how it began
:::

::: {.small}
| Emails counted | Hispanic names | White names | Difference |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Coded replies (n = 362) | 41.2% | 61.1% | −19.97 points |
| Delivered emails (n = 662) | 21.6% | 35.0% | −13.34 points |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Two defensible questions. Among the replies: the question of the claim, about tone, but an effect of the name alone only if the name did not change who replied. Among all emails: an effect of the name that randomisation protects, on a different outcome. The reply gap of −4.8 points (p = 0.214) makes a large selection unlikely, without ruling it out.
:::

::: notes
The remedy is to remove the box. Count every email that arrived, and treat an email that drew no reply as one that drew no greeting. Now nothing is conditioned on, and the groups are exactly as the random number generator made them. But the outcome has changed with the denominator: it is now a reply that greets the sender by name, which combines whether a reply came with how it began. Among replies, forty-one per cent against sixty-one, a gap of twenty points. Among all delivered emails, twenty-two against thirty-five, a gap of thirteen. [advance] Neither is wrong. The comparison among replies answers the question of the claim, about tone, and is clean only if the name did not change who replied. The comparison among all emails is clean by design, and answers a related but different question. One of the five analysts made exactly this move.
:::

## Model formulas {#a-model-is-a-formula-plus-data .smaller .deepdive run="tools"}

```{.r code-line-numbers="|1|3|5"}
named ~ hispanic                                    # "named explained by hispanic"

m <- lm(named ~ hispanic, data = replies)           # a linear model

g <- glm(named ~ hispanic, family = binomial(), data = replies)   # a logit
```

::: {.small}
The tilde `~` reads **outcome on the left, predictors on the right**; add predictors with `+`. Almost every modelling function in R has this shape: `something(formula, data = ...)`.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
With a 0/1 outcome and a 0/1 predictor, the coefficient of `lm()` **is** the difference between the two shares. Part 3 comes back to both models[, in the reproduction]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}.
:::

::: notes
A model in R is a formula plus data, and the tilde is the heart of the formula: outcome on the left, predictors on the right, more predictors added with a plus. Then lm fits a linear model, and glm with the binomial family fits a logistic regression, a logit. Almost every modelling function in R has this same shape, a formula and then data, so once you know it, lm, glm and everything after them become variations on one pattern. [advance] And one fact that makes this case easy to learn on: when the outcome is zero or one and the predictor is zero or one, the coefficient of the linear model is exactly the difference between the two shares. A greeting rate of forty-one per cent against sixty-one gives a coefficient of minus point two. One more lens: power, the probability that a study of a given size detects a gap of a given size. At a white share of sixty-one per cent, the original comparison, with about a hundred and eighty replies a group, detects a twenty-point gap almost every time. But its power for a ten-point gap is under one half, and for thirteen points about seven in ten. The replication, with three hundred and sixty-nine replies a group, has nearly eight in ten for ten points. Two consequences. A replication of this size would have found a gap of ten points about four times in five, and a larger one more often still, had there been one.
